payload.text: Initial-rate data show rate doubles when [A] doubles and quadruples when [B] doubles.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Determine the rate law and describe a compatible slow elementary step.

criteria.description: rate=k[A][B]^2; a compatible slow step must match this molecular dependence or follow a justified mechanism.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain how the method of initial rates (comparing rate ratios as [A] and [B] are varied) establishes the reaction orders, and state the assumption that the proposed slow step's molecularity matches the observed rate law.

criteria.description: The method of initial rates compares how rate changes as [A] and [B] are independently varied, assuming the proposed elementary step's molecularity matches the derived rate law.
accepted_variants: Equivalent scientifically correct notation and reasoning earn credit.
criteria.minimum_fix: To earn this point, explicitly show method of initial rates; molecularity assumption.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe how you would test the rate law experimentally, identifying the initial rate of B formation as the measured variable while holding [B] constant and varying only [A].

criteria.description: A valid check measures the initial rate while holding [B] constant and varying only [A] to isolate its order.
accepted_variants: Equivalent scientifically correct notation and reasoning earn credit.
criteria.minimum_fix: To earn this point, explicitly show initial rate measurement; [B] held constant.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: State one boundary case (e.g., a significant reverse reaction near equilibrium) and predict whether the measured initial rate would be too high or too low relative to the forward-only rate law.

criteria.description: A significant reverse reaction near equilibrium subtracts from the net forward rate, making the measured initial rate too low.
accepted_variants: Equivalent scientifically correct notation and reasoning earn credit.
criteria.minimum_fix: To earn this point, explicitly show reverse reaction; rate too low.
